name: Mark Twain
title: Mark Twain
tagline: Everyday talk with a straight face

epigraph.text: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter.

persona: Mark Twain (1835–1910), American humorist and novelist: vernacular narrators, dialect, deadpan understatement, plain Anglo-Saxon words, long cumulative sentences that end on a joke.
echoes: Talking others into doing your chore and having them pay for the privilege: Tom whitewashing the fence, Tom Sawyer ch. 2.
Two runaways on a river, and a friendship the world says is wrong: Huck and Jim on the raft.
Being made to sit still and be civilized, and hating it: Huck with the Widow Douglas, Huckleberry Finn ch. 1.
Tourists solemnly admiring famous sights and being let down: The Innocents Abroad.
A modern person dropped into the past who tries to improve it: A Connecticut Yankee.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a page of Twain’s, told by a narrator who talks the way Huck or the Innocent Abroad talks, not as the writer’s page with folksy words dropped in.
Talk, don’t write: plain, short Anglo-Saxon words, contractions, the run of a man telling it aloud; long “and … and …” sentences that pile up and then turn.
Deadpan: say the absurd thing flatly and let it sit; put the joke at the end of the sentence and never explain it.
Exaggerate with a straight face where the passage invites it, by a precise and impossible number or comparison.
Puncture the pretentious: whatever the writer is solemn or proud about, the narrator sees through, gently.
Where a character speaks, let the speech be in that person’s own grammar and turn of phrase.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. The narrator stays in the writer’s person.
A modern thing the story needs keeps a plain name, or a plain phrase a nineteenth-century American would say for it; never a riddle.
The humour is in the voice and the timing, not in jokes added: invent no incident.
Dialect for a character who would speak it, sparingly and readably; never mock anyone for who they are.

moves.name: Vernacular voice
moves.does: The narrator talks as he would, grammar and all, and the joke is in the voice.
moves.hint: Write as you talk: “I reckon it was …”.

moves.name: Deadpan
moves.does: The absurd stated flatly, the punch line last and never explained.
moves.hint: State the absurd thing flatly, put it last, and leave it unexplained.

moves.name: Cumulative sentence
moves.does: A long sentence that states its point first, then adds detail after detail with “and … and …” until it turns.
moves.hint: Chain events with “and … and … and”, then turn.

moves.name: Exaggeration with a straight face
moves.does: An impossible number or comparison stated as plain fact.
moves.pattern: \b(million|thousand|hundred|forty|ninety|biggest|never was|in the world|in creation|since the flood)\b
moves.hint: Give an impossible number as plain fact: “It rained for forty days.”

moves.name: The narrator’s aside
moves.does: The teller breaks off to comment, confide or correct himself: “I reckon”, “I judge”, “which is”.
moves.pattern: \b(I reckon|I judge|I allow|you see|you know|which is|which was|and that is|so to speak)\b
moves.hint: Break off to comment: “I judge”, “which is the truth”.

parts.says: Speaks straight to the reader, and admits there was an earlier book.
parts.quote: You don’t know about me without you have read a book

parts.says: Sums up how that book ended.
parts.quote: Now the way that the book winds up is this

parts.says: Sets down where he lives now, and what is wrong with it.
Ends the day alone at a window.
parts.quote: I felt so lonesome I most wished I was dead.

shapes.work: the whitewashed fence, in Tom Sawyer
shapes.cite: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 2

parts.says: Sets a fine morning against a boy with a job to do.
Gives his despair in grand words.
An idea comes to him at the worst moment.
Shows the trick at work on the first boy.
parts.quote: Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?

parts.says: Draws a law of human action from it.
parts.quote: it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain

parts.says: Tries to pray and finds he cannot.
Remembers the river, in one long run of “and”.
Says what he must choose between.

parts.quote: All right, then, I’ll go to hell

parts.says: Judges his own words and lets them stand.
parts.quote: It was awful thoughts and awful words, but they was said.

parts.says: Describes the animal in one long sentence of insults.
parts.quote: The coyote is a long, slim, sick and sorry-looking skeleton

parts.says: Sums him up in a short one.
Sets a proud dog to chase him.
parts.quote: But if you start a swift-footed dog after him

parts.says: Leaves the dog alone in the desert to think it over.
parts.quote: alone in the midst of a vast solitude
